questions.question: Why is every ordinary eigenvector also a generalized eigenvector?
options: It is automatically an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.
It already satisfies $(A-λI)v=0$, so k=1 works.
It satisfies $(A-λI)v=v$, so k=0 works.
It has to be linearly independent from all other eigenvectors.

questions.question: In defective matrices, what do generalized eigenvectors help replace?
options: Missing ordinary eigenvectors needed for a full basis.
Repeated eigenvalues, which they split into distinct ones.
Missing eigenvalues in the characteristic polynomial.
A missing inverse, since defective matrices are singular.

questions.question: Let $N=A-2I$. If $Nv≠0$ but $N^2v=0$, what is v for the eigenvalue 2?
options: An ordinary eigenvector of $A$ for the eigenvalue $4$
Not a generalized eigenvector, because $Nv\neq0$
An ordinary eigenvector, because $N^2v=0$ is enough
A generalized eigenvector, not an ordinary one

questions.question: Does the definition say that the same exponent k must work for every generalized eigenvector?
options: No. Some positive $k$ must work for that vector
Yes. $k$ must equal the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$
No. Any $k$ works, so one may always take $k=1$
Yes. $k=1$ for every vector, as for eigenvectors

questions.question: For the 3 by 3 Jordan block $J=\begin{pmatrix}4&1&0\\0&4&1\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is $(J-4I)(0,0,1)^{\top}$?
Why does the existence of generalized eigenvectors not by itself make a matrix diagonalizable?
options: A diagonal form needs $1$s on the superdiagonal of each block.
A diagonal form needs a basis made up of ordinary eigenvectors.
Generalized eigenvectors are never useful for any canonical form.
Generalized eigenvectors are always dependent, so never a basis.

questions.question: If $N=A-λI$ and the smallest positive exponent with $N^kv=0$ is $k=2$, which vector is an ordinary eigenvector for λ?
options: $Nv$

questions.question: Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of a square matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ and let $\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. When is $\boldsymbol{v}$ a generalized eigenvector of $\boldsymbol{A}$ for $\lambda$?
options: When $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})^k\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}$ for some positive integer $k$
When $\boldsymbol{A}^k\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ for some positive integer $k$
When $\boldsymbol{A}^k\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda^k\boldsymbol{v}$ for some positive integer $k$
When $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a square complex matrix and let $\mu\in\mathbb{C}$ be a number that is not an eigenvalue of $\boldsymbol{A}$. Can a nonzero vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ satisfy $(\boldsymbol{A}-\mu\boldsymbol{I})^3\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}$?
options: No, since $\boldsymbol{A}-\mu\boldsymbol{I}$ is invertible, so its cube is invertible too.
Yes, since higher powers of $\boldsymbol{A}-\mu\boldsymbol{I}$ can send more vectors to $\boldsymbol{0}$.
Yes, if $\boldsymbol{A}$ is defective, since it then needs vectors beyond its eigenvectors.
Yes, whenever $\mu^3$ is an eigenvalue of the matrix $\boldsymbol{A}^3$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, whose only eigenvalue is $3$. Which nonzero vectors $\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ are generalized eigenvectors of $\boldsymbol{A}$ for the eigenvalue $3$?
options: Only the nonzero multiples of $(0,1)^{\top}$
Only the vectors $\boldsymbol{v}=(v_1,v_2)^{\top}$ with $v_1\neq0$
Every nonzero vector $\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^2$
Only the nonzero multiples of $(1,0)^{\top}$ or of $(0,1)^{\top}$
